STATEMENT BY BRITISH PRIME MINISTER.
speechtext:
With the consent of the House, it might be

appropriate for me to read in this connection the announcement in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom by the Prime Minister with respect to the holding of an Imperial War Cabinet during the present year, and the proposal that it should be held annually in future. That announcement would not be readily available unless it is placed in Hansard, and as the announcement is of some importance, I think it might be well to record it in that way. The report reads:
Mr. McKenna:	May I ask the Prime Minister whether he has any statement to make in regard to the Imperial War Cabinet?
The Prime Minister (Mr. Lloyd George) :
I think that I ought to report to the House a very important decision that was arrived at as a sequel to the recent meetings of the Imperial War Cabinet. It is desirable that Parliament should be officially and formally acquainted with an event that will constitute a memorable landmark in the Constitutional History of the British Empire. The House will remember that in December last His Majesty's Government invited the Prime Ministers or leading statesmen of the Overseas Dominions and of India to attend the sittings both of the Cabinet and of an Imperial War Conference to be held in this country. It is to the former body which assembled In March, and held fourteen sittings before separating, that I desire to refer. The British Cabinet became for the time being an Imperial War Cabinet. While it was in session, its overseas members had access to all the information which was at the disposal of His Majesty's Government, and occupied a status of absolute equality with that of the members of the British War Cabinet. It had prolonged discussions on all the most vital aspects of Imperial policy, and came to important decisions in regard to them-decisions which will enable us to prosecute the war with increased unity and vigour, and which will be of the greatest value when it comes to the negotiations of peace. I should like to add on be-ha'f of the Government that the fresh minds and new points of view which our colleagues from over the seas have brought to bear upon the problems with which we have been so long engrossed, has been an immense help to us all. So far as we are concerned we can say with confidence that the experiment has been a complete success.
The conclusions of the Imperial War Cabinet are of necessity secret, but there is one aspect of them which we feel ought to be communicated to the House without delay. The Imperial War Cabinet was unanimous that the new procedure had been of such service, not only to all its members, but to the Empire, that it ought not to be allowed to fall into desuetude. Accordingly, at the last session, I proposed formally on behalf of the British Government that meetings of an Imperial Cabinet should be held annually or at any intermediate time when matters of urgent Imperial concern require to be settled, and that the Imperial Cabinet should consist of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, and such of his colleagues as deal specially with Imperial affairs; of the Prime Minister of each of the Dominions or some specially
accredited alternate possessed of equal authority: and of a representative of the Indian people to be appointed by the Government ot India. This proposal met with the cordial approval of. the overseas representatives and we hope that the holding of an annual Imperial Cabinet to discuss foreign affairs and other aspects of Imperial policy, will become an accepted convention of the British Constitution.
I ought to add that the institution in its present form is extremely elastic. It grew not by design, but out of the necessities of the war. The essence of it is that the responsible heads of the Governments of the Empire with those ministers who are specially entrusted with the conduct of Imperial policy should meet together at regular intervals to confer about foreign policy and matters connected therewith, and come to decisions in regard to them, which, subject to the control of their own Parliaments, they will then severally execute. By this means they will be able to obtain full information about all aspects of Imperial affairs and to determine, by consultation together the policy of the Empire in its most vital aspects, without infringing in any degree the autonomy which its parts at present enjoy. To what constitutional developments this may lead we did not attempt to settle. The whole question of perfecting the mechanism for continuous consultation about Imperial and foreign affairs between the autonomous nations of an Imperial Commonwealth will be reserved for the consideration of that special conference which will be summoned as soon as possible after the war to readjust the constitutional relations of the Empire. We felt, however, that the experiment of constituting an Imperial Cabinet, in which India was represented, had been so fruitful in better understanding and in unity of purpose and action that it ought to be perpetuated and we believe that this proposal will commend itself to the judgment of all the nations of the Empire.

speechtext:
The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) asked the number of Canadian troops in England, the number in France and the number in Canada. The answer is as follows:
1.	On the 4th June, 1917, there were 136,400 troops (all ranks) in France; there were also 747 in the Near East, and 130 at St. Lucia.
2.	On the 4th June, 1917, there were 108,736 troops (all ranks) in England-not counting those in hospitals and convalescent homes, but counting those on passage from Canada to England.
Of the foregoing total, however, only 26,000 men were immediately available for reinforcing purposes.
3.	On the 1st June, 1917, there were 17,353 C.E.P. troops (all ranks) in Canada.
I have a document illustrating the manner in which troops are classified in England, dated 14th May, 1917. I shall lay about sixty copies of it on the table of the House for the use of members.

speechtext: I would assume that if, upon the question which comes first irf order, as to whether there is evidence to justify the report, the commissioners should be of opinion that the assistance of counsel will be useful, they might, either on their own motion, or on the application of anybody who desires to be represented, permit the appearance of counsel. speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On tire Orders of the Day:
Mr. JOS. 'GIRARD (.Ohicoutimi-S ague-nav) (translation) : Mr. Speaker, before taking up the Orders of the Day, I desire to give a few personal explanations on some remarks that were made in this House on the 13th of June, and in which my name was mentioned, in connection with an item of 80,000 for a steamboat service between Rivi-erekiu-Loup, Tadoussac, etc. In the course of his remarks on that occasion, the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Gau-vreau) used the following words:
But, unfortunately, polities carried weight even in so serious a matter as this. In 1912, Mr. BfirubS was elected to the Local Legislature for Temiscouata and he happens to be a Conservative. Being unfriendly to the management of the company, he started at once

to oppose it. Then, there was the hon. member for Chicoutimi and Saguenay (Mr. Girard), a Conservative member on the North Shore. With these two warring against it, it is no wonder that the poor company was killed. The contract with that company was cancelled, and a contract was made with the Quebec and Levis Ferry Boat Company.
I wish to state to the House that my hon. friend's reference to me is utterly groundleSiS and contrary to the facts.
The hon. member for Temiscouata is aware that at the request of the TransSt. Lawrence Company I went to the cost of a trip to Fraserville in order to meet the officers of the company at the house of Dr. Perrot himself, who was, I surmise, president of the company, with a view to discussing the means of forestalling what did happen later on, the condemning of the boat by the Government officials. The meeting prepared a statement which I forwarded myself to the minister strongly urging its favourable consideration, I really did all I could to get the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Sir George Foster) to comply with their request, but he could not see his way to do it because it would entail an expenditure much greater than the ' appropriation. Some time later the Government officers pronounced the boat unfit for service naturally without my being advised or having any control over the matter. The company refused to put on another boat, and the Minister of Trade found that he could make arrangements with the company previously referred to, The Quebec and Levis Ferry Boat Company, who took over the contract which the Trans-St. Lawrence Company could not carry out. An accident happened, true, but the new company put another boat on the line until the expiry of the contract. I think it only fair to state that the accident referred to could have happened to the Mahone, which had less power.
The member for Temiscouata further stated that the second boat was wrecked in St. Catherine's bay, I fail to see where he got that information, as no such thing ever took place.
Later on, the Government called for tenders for that service; tenders were put in but all for a larger amount than the appropriation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: STEAMSHIP' SERVICE BETWEEN RIVI-ERE-DU-LOUP AND THE NORTH SHORE.
speechtext: I regret to have to interrupt the hon. member, but in making a personal explanation he should adhere as closely as possible to the statement complained of.

maintopic: STEAMSHIP' SERVICE BETWEEN RIVI-ERE-DU-LOUP AND THE NORTH SHORE.
speechtext:
I am just about finishing, Mr. Speaker.

The minister always refused to consider any increase of the subsidy because at the present time the Government does not wish to incur new expenditure. Jointly with the Government I tried in every possible way to meet the needs of that district, of both the counties of Temiscouata and Saguenay, but up to date, we have been unable to find a man or a company who cared to take up the contract for the amount of the subsidy.
Such are the facts, and I wish to deny most emphatically the imputation against me of the hon. member for Temiscouata, namely that party politics are responsible for the failure of the company.
I, for one, and my constituency, are above such petty tactics; as to what is the rule with him, I have no idea and leave him to settle the matter with his own electors.

There is a reduction of $4,387.50 under the heading of salaries. This is largely accounted for by the fact that there is no Clerk of Eoutine and Eecords, the work of that office being performed by the former assistant, who still holds the rank of Assistant Clerk of Eoutine and Eecords. So far as I can ascertain, the work of the office is being satisfactorily performed by the present staff, and unless some good reason arises for an additional appointment, this saving may be continued indefinitely. Further, according to the Civil Service regulation, the salary of the Assistant Clerk begins at a certain figure and increases by increments of $100 a year. His salary, therefore, is not as large as was the salary of the Assistant Clerk whom he succeeded. These two items account largely, if not entirely, for the reduction.

The reduction in this vote is a temptation to us to appoint a permanent Speaker. A reduction of this amount in the expenses of the House at the hands of our Speaker is, in my view, a strong recommendation for the continuance of that gentleman in office.
Mr. MAECIL; Could the Speaker give us an explanation of the circumstances under which the Chief French Translator, Mr. Laframboise, was superannuated?

That was done before
I took office, and I am not familiar with the circumstances. If the hon. member
wishes me to do so, I sha'l make careful inquiry and advise him later.

I understand that Mr. Laframboise is still in splendid health, quite capable of doing his work, and probably as efficient as ever. Can the Speaker tell us who replaced him, and what changes were made in the office?

Mr. Desaulniers, next
in rank, was promoted to the position formerly occupied by Mr. Laframboise. I must make further inquiry before I can give my hon. friend a satisfactory answer.
Legislation-General, $346,600.

There are two increases here, one of $6,000 and another of $2,000. They arise solely on account of the increased cost .of paper and of printing, larger sums being required to do slightly less work and to furnish less supplies than in former years. Further, the stock was considerably depleted by the fire.

Would it not be possible for the Speaker to appeal to the Minister ,of Finance for a restriction on the high price of paper, so that this estimate might show the same good tendency towards reduction as the previous one?

These items come from the office of the Secretary of State. My information is that the Speaker has never been responsible in any degree for their *amount. To be perfectly candid, I never saw these items until they appeared in the Estimates.

It might be a good idea
to suggest that this vote be placed under the control of the Speaker in the future.

The work under this
vote is done by the Printing Bureau, which, as the hon. member knows, has always been under the Secretary of State; and which accounts for this item appearing in the Estimates as coming from that branch of the Government. It is somewhat of an anomaly, I must admit, that work for which, the Speaker is not responsible should appear in the Estimates in this way.

In this and the preceding item the Speaker has been able to effect a substantial reduction, but as soon as we pass to an item not under his control the cost increases. It almost looks as if the Department of Public Printing and Stationery were trying to put one over the House of Commons and the Speaker, and I would respectfully suggest that in the future this item be placed under the control of his

Honour, so that he may deal with the department from an independent standpoint and secure the same measure of economy and efficiency he has brought about in other departments under his control. There-is no reason why the House of Commons should allow the Department of Public Printing and Stationery to take advantage of circumstances.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, in Montreal. The district of Montreal under my department is the largest in Canada. In that district we collect over $10,000,000 a year, which is more than we collect in all the other districts of Canada combined. We have been compelled to increase the number of our employees in the district of Montreal.

Could the minister give
us the names of the new appointments? Or I would ask that later if he would prefer it

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I would prefer that.
Meantime I will get the names from the department.

I would suggest that the minister should stick to the item before us, which is the vote for the Inside Service for his department. In his Excise Branch, he has added two employees with an additional charge for salaries of $2,588 a year. In his Laboratory Branch, he has three new employees with an addition of $3,750. Then under the head of contingencies, he has an increase of $1,900 for printing and stationery, and $100 for clerical assistance. I would like the minister to take up each of these branches and explain who has been added to the staff, and why. He tells us generally that the increase is on account of the War Revenues Act. That,
I suppose, means the collection of stamps*. But that does not seem to me any particular reason for adding to the number of the Inside Service. Every minister except the hon. gentleman himself has decreased his Estimates, while he has made an increase of nearly $10,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
As to The increase of
$100 for clerical service, I am told by my deputy minister that that is only to make a round figure.

Why did you not
make it "three hundred," it would look just as pretty?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I admit that, but that would be more than sufficient for our requirements.

What about the
$6,000 for printing and stationery?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: In some of the departments the expenditure has been reduced, but the Customs Department and my department, since the war broke out, have been called upon to supply a large amount of money to the Government, and our revenues have increased to a large extent. In my department, as in every other business, when affairs are prosperous and we are making money, we have to spend more money. We require more stationery on account of the new laws which have been passed and the new revenues which we have to collect.
The Customs Department is not asking any more for printing than they did last year, and it is making more money than your department.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I suppose the Customs Department had everything it wanted before. The other item, $12,000, is the same as it was last year.
I saw in a newspaper the other day that Mr. Raoul Renault of Quebec had been appointed an accountant in the Department of Inland Revenue. Is that true?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No, Mr. Raoul Renault was recommended for the position, and the Civil Service Commission refused to give him a certificate.
Did the minister recommend Mr. Renault himself?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I thought that Mr. Renault was perfectly qualified for the position, and I made the recommendation, but the Civil Service Commission refused to accept him.

I suppose the recommendation made by the minister of Mr. Renault does not mean that he endorses Mr. Renault's ideas as expressed in his newspaper in Quebec with regard to recruiting and other matters relating to the war?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know Mr. Renault's opinions on the war. I know that on many occasions he has condemned some papers of our province for the expressions of opinion on the war, and from what I can gather, Mr. Renault is willing to support every measure submitted by the Government to aid the Allies in this war.

Did the minister
read Mr. Renault's paper, Le Franc Par-leur, last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No.

1 know that Mr. Renault, especially with regard to the recruiting of the 171st Regiment, under the command of Sir William Price, had very violent articles against that officer, and strongly advised people not to enlist, at least in that regiment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am not surprised at that because Mr. Renault and Sir William Price are not very good friends; in fact, they are the reverse; but if any attacks were made by Mr. Renault upon Sir William Price, I do not think the Minister of Inland Revenue is responsible for that. Sir William Price is a good friend of mine; he has my admiration, and when he was raising his regiment, I endeavoured to assist him. Now, my hon. friend can put any more question about Mr. Renault, but that gentleman is not appointed, and the Civil Service Commission having refused to give him a certificate, he will not be appointed.
Shall the item be carried?
No.

Section 5 of rule 13 states that:
Speeches in Committee of the Whole must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration.
I do not consider that these statements come under that rule.
Are we not discussing an item relating to salaries of the department of which the minister is head?
Yes.
And is not this discussion relating to the merits of appointments to that department?

The item before the committee is "Department of Inland Revenue, salaries, $180,412.50, and contingencies, $22,000." Speeches in Committee of the Whole must be strictly relevant to the item or clause under consideration. 1 do not think that a discussion on statements in regard to Mr. Renault's opinion on the w'ar published in his newspaper would come within the rule. I understand the minister to say that the gentleman spoken of is not in the emplby of the Government.
The minister said that he recommended Mr. Renault.

Inasmuch as this is an item covering salaries in the Department of Inland Revenue, the appointment of men to serve in that department is necessarily pertinent to the discussion of the appropriation. In regard to the gentleman under discussion, I understand from the minister that he considered him a suitable person for employment in the department, and that, as a matter of fact, he did appoint him, but that his appointment was not confirmed by the Civil Service Commission. The point taken by my hon. friend from Kamouraska, as I understood it, and certainly the point that I would wish to take, was that a gentleman, who is the editor of a newspaper and who uses that paper during this time of war for discouraging efforts towards the winning of the war, is not a suitable person to be recommended by the minister for a salaried position under this Government, and we take exception to the minister's recommendation of that gentleman for that position.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Renault was not appointed by me; he was recommended by me. It is true that a certain paper, Le Franc Parleur, was published in the city of Qu ebec.
What is the translation of that name?
The Plain Speaker.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: In my judgment, it was certainly regrettable to have in that paper, especially during this crisis, certain articles, and to put an end to that, I thought it would be a good thing to close the paper.

To give him a good
job.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Not necessarily a good
job, but at the same time it would be in the public interest if papers like Le Franc Parleur or La Liberte at Montreal or some other papers were closed at the present time and if such papers

Are you going to
give him a job too?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No, if I give him a job it will be in jail.

Perhaps he is not yet
thirty years of age, he may be a young man.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Perhaps. Mr. Renault
was mentioned for a position in my depart-

ment, not a new position, but that of accountant, which is vacant, and I can assure my hon. friend that I made that recommendation especially for one reason. I owed nothing to Mr. Renault, but I thought that it would be a good thing if such a paper could be put out of existence in this crisis.

Hear, hear, instead
of putting him in jail-
Make Bourassa a deputy minister.

I should like to draw the minister's attention to the fact that there are other means of dealing with newspapers which make improper references at this particular time. I have in mind a newspaper at Sault Ste. Marie which was suppressed by the authorities because of the character of its utterances, although I have no knowledge of the nature of those utterances. It is certainly a somewhat remarkable fact that at Sault Ste. Marie a newspaper is suppressed because of its utterances, and in the favoured locality that my hon. friend has the honour to represent, in a general if not in a particular way, such utterances are suppressed by appointment to a Government position, or by recommendation for a Government position, at, I presume, a fair salary. That appears to me to be such a wide difference of treatment between parallel instances that it surely cannot be allowed to pass without unfavourable comment at the hands of this Parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: First, perhaps, it would be better to know what the utterances of the paper in Quebec were. Perhaps there was some animosity between Mr. Renault and Sir William Price, but, as I said at first, I think that Mr. Renault, since the beginning of this war, has always been well disposed to do everything possible to help the Allies, and I do not think that paper, La Franc Parleur, ever criticised our participation in this war. Perhaps some articles in that paper tvere not in the public interest, especially in the city of Quebec. I do not know if they were written by Mr. Renault or by some other man.
He would be responsible for them if they were in his paper.

Along what lines did
the articles proceed?
I am going to ask the committee to assist the Chair in keeping somewhere near the subject before the committee. I am sure hon. gentlemen will do that.

The committee, of course, desire to keep within the rules, and we will not refuse to abide by the ultimate decision of the Chair; but the ruling should at least be fair. We are simp'y discussing what is the policy of the department.
Does my hon. friend say that the ruling is not fair?

No, I do not say it is not fair. We are now discussing the policy of the department in respect to the appointment of officials. The minister has declared, in a fair manner, that it is his policy to bring into the service persons engaged! in newspaper work who might possibly be charged with writing seditious articles. Apparently it is the minister's policy that it is in the interest of the country to withdraw these dangerous men from their profession and put them into the public service. If a man is engaged in a dangerous propaganda in these days, in newspaper work, it is a question of policy, a fair question of argument for the committee to decide whether the policy of the department is right or wrong, and whether such men should be introduced into the public service. The salaries of the department are being voted, and surely it is a fair thing for us on this side to say that the minister has enunciated a very improper policy. Some men would argue, and with fairness I think, that if a man is engaged in writing seditious articles in the press he should be prosecuted or should be put in jail. The minister says: I will take them into the service and let them become servants of the King. I submit that that is a fair mattter for discussion, and I say that the policy of the minister is wrong. I was going to ask the minister if he had any understanding with Mr. Renault that, if he -came into the service of the Grown, he would abstain from writing questionable or seditious articles. Did the minister discuss it with the commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I wish to say this: I do not think it is fair for the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. A. K. Maclean) to say that Mr. Renault, to the knowledge of the Minister of Inland Revenue, was writing seditious articles. That is not true. If seditious articles were written by Mr. Renault, it is not to my knowledge.

I will withdraw the word "seditious;" perhaps that is not correct. But the minister himself expressed the view that he was engaged in writing



articles of some nature that were objectionable to him, and he deemed it advisable to withdraw him from that sphere of activity and put him into the public service. The articles were apparently with reference to recruiting. I withdraw the word "seditious," but that does not detract from the position I take.

I am going to ask the committee to decide whether or not they think this discussion is on the item before the Chair, and if there is any hon. gentleman who wants to appeal from the Chair's decision, he has a perfect right to do so. But I propose to stop this kind of discussion.
Then I would desire to make the appeal from the decision of the Chair.

Perhaps you will . bear with me while I say in justice to Mr. Renault that while I believe he would be a qualified officer so far as aptitude and abilities are concerned, I really think that his opinions at the present time, and the opinions he has avowed for the last two years, are not of a nature to recommend him to my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue since his conversion from Nationalist principles.

It would be well for the committee to understand just what this ruling is. I do not understand the Chair to make any particular decision, but to leave it open to himself to decide when a discussion is germane to the point. I would think it a dangerous ruling to say that we are not permitted to discuss the policy of aDpointments.
I will leave it to the fair play of the members in the House, to say whether they propose to discuss under this item, newspaper articles on the w,ar.
We wero not discussing newspaper articles.
Order. Or whether we shall discuss matters dealing with the war.

Will the chairman
state what his ruling is?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: My ruling was given and it is not for the hon. gentleman from Pietou to say.
Yes it is.

I am in the Chair. I call "Order," and the hon.

gentleman can appeal to the Speaker. 1 have given my decision, and I will leave it to the House to say whether a discussion of this kind, dealing with newspaper articles or the expressions of the editor in regard to the *war, comes within the item before the Chair. If my hon. friend wishes to appeal from my decision, he has the right.

I am not familiar with the rules of the House, but I desire to appeal, and take a vote of the committee. I was under the impression that an appeal must be taken without discussion. If there is opportunity for discussion, I wish to place before the committee, as shortly as possible, my view of the subject.
The appeal is to the Speaker, and not to the chairman.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I have no objection to
give -all explanations required from me as to this recommendation.
But the chairman will not let you do so.

The minister admits he
recommended this gentleman for appointment. I think, in doing so-, he was helping a good cause, namely recruiting, by putting an end to a certain campaign in Quebec more or less injurious to recruiting.
I understood all that.
The question the committee is discussing is whether the minister was wise in recommending such a gentleman.

I have already decided that the statement of the minister, and the other statements in answer, are out of order, and I appeal to the good sense of the committee to say whether they think this kind of discussion should continue.
We are appealing.
I am quite willing you should appeal.
How is the newspaper article mixed up with it?
Order, order.

Would the Chairman
explain in what way the newspaper becomes part of this point of order?

A statement was made by my hon. friend from Kamouraska (Mr. Lapointe) that a certain

newspaper article expressed an opinion of a man who made application to the minister for a position, and the point in the hon. gentleman's statement was his expression in regard to the war, whether it was for the war or against the war, and I ruled that that kind of discussion was out of order.
That is not the point.
I know that is not my hon. friend's idea, but I am giving my decision. If the hon. gentleman from Edmonton (Mr. Oliver) wishes to appeal from my ruling, he can do so.
I desire to appeal from the ruling of the Chair, and I ask the privilege of stating my view of the subject
The hon. gentleman can state it to the Speaker.
I move that the committee rise.
All those in favour of the motion say, Aye.

I am not familiar with
the rules. I understood an appeal from the Chairman's ruling went automatically to the House.
There is a motion before the committee.
I move that the committee rise.

Is it the pleasure of hon. gentlemen that the committee rise and report to the Speaker?
Mr, MAROIL:	According to thq procedure, when an hon. member appeals from the Chairman's decision, it is the duty of the Chairman to report to the Speaker.
I am not very familiar with the rule myself. I will report to the Speaker.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I ask the
Chairman to read the report he proposes to make to the Speaker because we may not be agreed on the statement.

My report to the Speaker reads as follows:
On the debate on the resolution No. 14, which reads as follows:
That a sum not exceeding $202,412.50 be granted to His Majesty for civil government.
Department of Inland Revenue-Salaries, $180,412.50; contingencies, $22,000.
Mr. Lapointe (Kamouraska) referred to certain articles published in Le Franc Parleur, a newspaper published in Quebec, and the Chairman ruled him out of order under Rule 13, paragraph 5. Mr. Oliver appeals to the House from this decision.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: It seems to me that that is hardly a sufficient reference. I was not in the House, but I understand that the minister was questioned as to his recommendation of the appointment of a certain Mr. Renault.

I do not wish to be discourteous to the right hon. leader of the Opposition, but I hardly have opportunity of discussing the matter with him. I made this ruling much against my will, but we must maintain order in the committee.

I am not able to agree that the statement presented by the Chairman is a correct one. The subject of discussion was the proposed appointment of a gentleman to earn part of the salary being voted, and his fitness for the position as shown by articles published in a newspaper which he edited.

On that point I did not rule my hon. friend out of order. When he reached the point where he stated that the article expressed an opinion on the war I then ruled him out of order. I did not rule the hon. member out of order on the question of his discussing the fitness of the man for the position; on the contrary, I decided that that was perfectly in order.

Our point was that this man, in his newspaper, used language that was not in the public interest, and that that was the reason given by the minister for recommending his appointment. We considered that that was an objection to his appointment, not a recommendation, and we were arguing accordingly.
I ruled that all out of order, the minister's statement as well as my hon. friend's.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I took the precaution to say that I did not know what articles were published by Mr. Renault in Le Franc Par-leur. If reprehensible articles were written by Mr. Renault, I have no knowledge of them. I said only this:	That there were
some difficulties between Mr. Renault and Sir William Price. Sir William Price is not the people of Canada, nor is he to decide whether or not we are to participate in this war. If there is a difference between Sir William Price and Mr. Renault, that does not mean that Mr. Renault has written sedi-

tious articles against our participation in the war.
You prevent him from writing any more hy giving him this job.

If I may refresh the minister's memory, the discussion was in this form: Sir William Price was raising a regiment, and the criticism offered by this man in his paper against the raising of a regiment by Sir William Price was the cause of his being recommended for the position-on the understanding that he should not publish such articles. Surely my hon. friend does not wish the committee to understand that he used the public service as a means of preventing discussion among his friends. He surely gave us to understand that he recommended the appointment because it was in the public interest that such discussion should be suppressed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Renault was recommended to me by the best business men of Quebec city, who told me that he was a very good accountant. Besides, I know personally that Mr. Renault has good qualifications as an accountant. An accountant is required in my department; the position is still vacant. I have recommended Mr. Renault, because he is perfectly qualified for the position. If some articles were written by Mr Renault in Le Franc Parleur, I do not know of them. I know that there is in Quebec a weekly newspaper called Le Franc Parleur. I do not know who is the owner, hut I can say this: If such a paper-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons

a question.	I simply wanted to ask
