Mr. Rainville takes the Chair.
Mr. E. LAPlOINTE:	Has anybody been
appointed as accountant yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Not yet.

I understand that
the chief qualification of Mr. Renault, beyond being an accountant, was that the minister desired to remove him from the

political arena where he was writing letters. for the purpose of discouraging enlistment in the regiment of Sir William Price. If that is the policy of the Government- to recommend for positions under the Government, people who write articles seeking to discourage voluntary recruiting and aiding Great Britain in the war-it is a policy that deserves the condemnation of the people of this country. If the ministers of the Crown are thus putting a premium on the conduct of men who are asking the people of the province of Quebec not to enlist, it readily explains the state of recruiting in that province. This method of dealing with people who make seditious speeches or write seditious articles in the province of Quebec will put this Government in a very peculiar position before the people of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Renault was recommended to the position because he was an accountant of long experience. He is about 50 years old.
I think most of his time he has been editing a newspaper.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
No. During the last
few months Mr. Renault has been writing certain articles in a weekly newspaper in Quebec.
Does my hon. friend say he has been editor of that paper for only the last two months?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The last few months.
He has been publishing that newspaper for at least three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I do not know about
that. I recommended him because in my judgment he was very well qualified for the position of accountant.

Who recommended
him to you?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Mr. J. Gignac, one of
the largest lumbermen in the city of Quebec, J. B. Letellier and J. M. Fortier.
Is it true that this man has been writing articles in the press against recruiting in the province of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: No.
You said so yourself just now.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I said just the contrary. I said that since the war broke out I understood that Mr. Renault had approved of Canada's participation in the war to the fullest possible extent.
I cannot permit the minister to change his statement. He said that this man had written articles in this newspaper with the object of discouraging enlistment in the regiment of Sir William Price.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I did not say that. I
said there was a quarrel between Sir William Price and Mr. Renault, that Mr. Renault had said some things about Sir William Price that perhaps were not over nice, and that Sir William Price may have reciprocated.
The minister certainly stated that this man had written articles urging men not to enlist in Sir William Price's regiment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I have never seen any
of these letters in Le Franc Parleur.
Now you are dodging.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know that Mr. Renault ever advised anybody not to enlist in that regiment.

You said so just
now.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I did not. My hon.
friend suggested that I recommended Mr. Renault because recruiting was not very active in the province of Quebec.
Did not the minister say he thought it well to give Mr. Renault this position, to prevent him writing further articles in that newspaper?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
If the appointment of
Mr. Renault had that effect, I think it would be a good thing. If recruiting has not been satisfactory in the province of Quebec it may be because of certain appeals which have been made, not by Mr. Renault, but by other people-for instance, the Liberal candidate in Dorchester at the recent election.

Did Mr. Renault own
or control the newspaper in which these appeals were made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know.

The minister suggested that the discouraging recruiting figures in the province of Quebec are due to certain statements made by the Liberal candidate in Dorchester.

Mr. SEVI'GNY: Yes, Mr. Cannon.
Did not the minister himself state in that campaign that when he was only 30, he had made anti-British appeals which he afterwards regretted? He has nothing on Mr. Cannon on that score.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Since the war broke
out I have done the best I could to secure Canada's participation in this war, and I intend to do so in the future. I hope my example will be followed by many hon. gentlemen opposite.

I do not think the time will ever come when hon. gentlemen on this side of the House will sit at the feet of the minister,, learning how to aid the Empire. Does not the minister think that the appeals he made five years ago against aiding Great Britain may still be having their effect, and possibly furnish an explanation for the failure of recruiting in Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
In 1910 I was very
strongly opposed to the naval policy of the Liberal party, but I have never .at any time made any appeals against Great Britain.

In justice to Mr. Cannon, who is a friend of mine, I must protest against the hon. member for Moose-jaw comparing his utterances in the recent election with those of the Minister of Inland Revenue in 1911. During the Drum-mond-Arthabaska election the present Minister of Inland Revenue said, " The Bill refers to the navy of His Majesty. Who is His Majesty? We have no Majesty in Canada." Mr. Cannon never said anything like that in Dorchester or anywhere else. He was one of the men who fought against the Minister of Inland Revenue and against the Postmaster General .and the Nationalists in 1911.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am .afraid that the ruling which has just been confirmed by so large a majority is in danger of being toppled over if this discussion continues. Do not hon. gentlemen think that we have had enough of this and that we had better go on with salaries?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I
would ask the committee to confine itself strictly to the item under discussion.

How far can we go in a discussion of a recommendation for an appointment of this kind? -What are the rights of the committee?
TMr. Knowles.!

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Marcil) has been Speaker- of the House and he ought not to put queries such as that. He knows very well.
It is only fair to say that the ruling which has been given, and which has been supported by a majority of the House, disarranges all former ideas as to what the Rules of the House mean.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If it is a matter of disarranging some of the talk that goes on upon the Estimates, do not we know in ouf hearts that it is a good disarrangement? Why not get on with the Estimates?

The remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton (Mr. Oliver), I think, call .for 'a statement to be made by somebody. The decision of the Chair, sustained by a vote of the House, was, briefly, on the question whether a reference to the opinion of an editor on the war published in a newspaper was relevant to a discussion of the estimates of the Department of Inland Revenue.
Oh, oh.
Nobody knows better than the gentleman (Mr. Blain), who has just spoken, that the way in which he put the question to the House was not the way in which the question was raised.
I put the question exactly as it was, and my hon. friend (Mr. Macdonald) knows it just as well as any other member of the House.
I wish the committee would keep to the Rules.

Before the Chairman ruled I put the question straight, whether it was open to us to discuss the policy of appointments by the minister, and the answer was that that was open to us. I take this to include the character and record of the men selected for appointment. I understood the Acting Chairman to say that we were within our rights in calling attention to these -matters. But he objected to a certain newspaper article toeing mentioned, and the'House sustained him in his ruling-
I will not say whether I think that was right or wrong. The principle was admitted by the Acting Chairman (Mr. Blain), and I presume will 'be admitted by you, Mr. Chairman, that we have the right to discuss the policy of any minister as to the kind of people that he will call to the Civil Service of this country. And that is what we are doing. I was startled by the announcement, made by the minister, that he thought it

was necessary to put an end to the articles appearing in a newspaper in Quebec which were detrimental to the best interests of recruiting and to the winning of the war, and the way he took to stop them was to bring the author of them into the Civil Service and into the heart of his department. That was to me startling- that any man whose conduct was such as to make him a danger to the country, a firebrand, had to be given the King's money and the King's appointment in order to take him out of the way. That is what started the discussion here to-day. But we need hardly be surprised that the minister followed that course, for he is a product of that line of action himself; he owes his position in the Cabinet to just such reasoning. When the right hon. gentleman (Sir George Foster), who leads the House, gave out the slogan in 1910, "Anything to beat Laurier " he announced a policy the chickens of which are coming home to roost. I't would be a strange thing indeed if we are not permitted in this House to call the attention of the minister to the fact that he is giving the reward of iniquity to the man he is calling to he an officer of Government. If this man, who was threatening sedition, did not come into the Service, it was not because the minister did not try to bring him in. He went as far as he could, but a commission, whose members, perhaps, knew more than the minister, turned him down. The fact that this man is not today receiving a reward for his flagitious conduct is not the fault of the minister; he was willing that such a man should come into, his department, and possess the secrets of that department, to spread them abroad, perhaps, against the interests of recruiting and to neutralize the efforts put forth to win the war. I hope we shall not hear again of efforts of that kind by the Minister of Inland Revenue, or any other minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) has referred to what took place in 1910 and 1911. In 1911, I was elected in the county of Dorchester. Two years after I came to this House I was asked by the Prime Minister to vote a contribution of $35,000,000 to help the British Naviy and increase the strength of the British Empire. At that time the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Sevigny), the French-Canadian, the "bad Nationalist," as he had been called by certain members of this House, voted for this .contribution-of $35,000,000 to help the British Empire, 'but the records
show that there were members of this .House sitting on the other side who refused to vote for that contribution. I repeat what I said a few minutes ago, that since the war broke out I have done everything possible to help recruiting and to promote the participation of Canada in the war; and it is my intention to do the same in the future. If the hon. member for North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) turns his attention to current events in the province of Quebec, he will see that the press of his own party in that province is doing worse than was done in 1910 and 1911. The excuse that might be pleaded for the people of 1910 and 1911 was that we were not at war; nobody knew what was coming. Nobody knew' what was coming, but at the present time every one knows what is going on and that we are in the greatest crisis of our history; and yet all the French press of the Libera] party in Quebec is repeating exactly-
It is out of order to refer to the press.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: -the same things w'hich are published every day by Mr. Tanerede Marsil and Mr. Bourassa.	-

The minister is certainly not representing the facts as they are when he dares to say in this House of Commons that the Liberal press of the province of Quebec is to-day using the same line of abuse that he used in 1910 and 1911.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The Liberal press is using it.

I challenge my hon. friend to show any newspaper representing liberal opinion in the province of Quebec which has ever published, either before the war started or during the war, such statements as I have mentioned a few minutes ago to have been uttered by the hon. gentleman and his friends in that province. The reverse is the ease. The Liberal press, from the outbreak of hostilities, has always advocated the participation of Canada in the war. The doctrine that the Liberal press is preaching to-day in Quebec is the same doctrine as that on which we went to the people in 1911, and upon whicn we asked the people of Quebec to return to this Parliament members supporting the right hon. gentleman who, in that province as throughout the rest of Canada, advocated the participation of Canada in the wars of the Empire in time of danger, and the taking of the necessary steps for giving adequate defence to Canada at any time.
What about the Liberal clubs?
The minister is speaking to-day of those who are using violent words in Quebec. Who are they? They are those who were going on the platforms with the minister in 1910 and 1911.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: All Liberals.

My hon. friend speaks of Mr. Tancrede Marsil. He was the Conservative Nationalist candidate in the county of Bagot in the election of 1911, and he said there what he is saying to-day in the city of Montreal. Who is using those violent words to-day of which my hon. friend is complaining? Mr. Lavergne.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: A good Liberal.
Mr. Lavergne was my hon. friend's friend in 1910 and 1911.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: He is your friend now.

He was your leader. He is not my leader. I have a leader of whom I am proud; I supported him in 1911; I have followed him in opposition, and to-day I am proud to follow him in the stand he has taken since the beginning of the war. I did not want, Sir, to be responsible for the little storm that has occurred in the House to-day, I assure you, but unfortunately the yery innocent remarks I made gave rise to this debate. I simply asked whether Mr. Renault had been appointed to the Department of Inland Revenue, because I saw that statement in the press the other day, and my hon. friend said that Mr. Renault had not been appointed; that he had been recommended by the Minister of Inland Revenue, but that the appointment was refused by the Civil Service Commission on account of Mr. Renault's age. I did not say anything against Mr. Renault's qualification, but I thought it rather strange that Mr. Renault, whose opinions, which are absolutely on the side' of nationalism, and which have been of that nature since he started publishing his newspaper, are well known in Quebec, should have been selected by the minister for such an important position in his department. I did not say that Mr. Renault had been seditious; it is the minister who has insinuated and hinted that to this House by saying that Mr. Renault's paper has been publishing articles that were an obstacle to recruiting in Quebec, and that it was in order to stop that, that the minister recommended his appointment to a position 
in the department. I think the minister is responsible for what has happened in this committee ihis afternoon.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I understand why these attacks are made by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. E. Lapointe). I stated a few minutes ago that the Liberal party in the province of Quebec are much worse than the Nationalists of 1910 and 1911 were; that in 1910 and 1911 no one knew what was coming, but that to-day every one knows that we are in a crisis of our history.
Mr. Chairman, I rise to a point of order. The attitude of :;he Liberal party in the province of Quebec has nothing to do with the item before the Chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is true-
I ask for a ruling on that point. We have already been requested to adhere to the item under discussion.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order is well taken.
May I ask the minister a question with regard to what he stated before he sat down? When he stated that the Liberal party in the province of Quebec-
Order.
-was more disloyal than the Nationalists in 1911, did he mean all the Liberal party or how much of it?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. That is absolutely out of order.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am willing to answer the question.
The whole Liberal party?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The Liberal party of the province of Quebec, and I can prove my statement in two minutes from the newspaper I have in my hand.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. This is out of order.
Is the minister going to prove that some one else was more disloyal than he was in 1910?
That is what he said.

I would like to know why Mr. Renault was recommended by the minister. I have here Le Franc Parleur, and I could read an extract from it to show that Mr. Renault did not oppose recruiting in Quebec at all. What Mr. Renault opposed

in Quebec was the way in which the Militia Department treated the French Canadian regiments in the district of Quebec. He said that Sir William Price had been given preferential treatment, and that with all the support of the department he had been able, after two years' efforts, to recruit only 550 men in the whole district, and that the French Canadian regiments commanded by Gol. Headman and Col. Piuze had not been given fair treatment and still had done better than Sir William Price had done. He stated that both these regiments had been disbanded, and that the soldiers who had enlisted in them had been drafted under false pretenses after a formal promise had been given that they would go to the front under French Canadian officers in French Canadian regiments, preserving their own identity. In this edition of his newspaper of the 9th of June, Mr. Renault objects to the recruiting methods of the Militia Department in the district of Quebec, and not to recruiting per se. In justice to this newspaper man-I belong to the craft-I thought I would make his statement plain. If the minister wishes to aid recruiting in Quebec, he should read what Mr. Renault says and apply his methods, so far as recruiting is concerned, to the Militia Department.
If the Board of Civil Service Commissioners should report Mr. Renault as qualified for the position, will the minister still appoint him?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not see what is the purpose of that question. I have given my answer that Mr. Renault was not the accountant of my department, that he was not appointed, and the matter is ended there.

Was the minister aware
when he made the recommendation that according to the regulations of the Civil Service no person over thirty-five years of age could be admitted into the service- of his department?
Mr. SEVI'GNY:	Yes, I was aware of
that, but in certain cases, as my hon. friend probably knows, when it is a technical position, this rule does not apply.
Does the minister think that the service of an accountant comes within the meaning of section 21 providing for the appointment of experts?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, it is considered as such by the Civil Service Commission.
Then why did not the Civil Service Commission accept the appointment?	*

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
If I remember aright,
they declared that Mr. Renault had not had enough experience to take the position.
Then he was not an expert in the opinion of the Civil Service Commission.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: He was not well enough qualified for the position.

Then the minister admits
that he tried to impose upon the department an expert who was not an expert.
Mr. iSEVIiGNY : The minister is not an accountant himself; but Mr. Renault was recommended to the minister by the best business men of the city of Quebec who told the minister that Mr. Renault was a very, very good accountant. The Civil -Service Commission have declared that Mr. Renault had not enough experience in departmental affairs.
What has become of the appointment, who got the office?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It is still vacant.
Mr. MARiOIL:	No appointment was
made from Ottawa of Mr. Laverdure? ,

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
No.
iMr. KNOWLES: Even' if the committee is not divided on this vote, I wish to place myself on record against passing this item. I do this for two reasons. In the first place, I am against voting money to the minister to be expended under a policy such as has been laid down. Humble member as a person may be, every one of us stands on an equal footing when he comes to register his vote, and I wish to be no party to voting money to be placed in the hands of this minister if he is going to alienate the people's money for reasons and on policies and principles such as he has laid down. He is the judge, and he is responsible. I will not say an unkind word about him, but I say that for my part I disapprove of money being voted under these circumstances. He told us clearly and plainly that the reason he recommended this gentleman was that he was writing certain articles which he thought were against our country's interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is not fair.
I heard the minister say-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is not fair, and you know it.

The minister can say it is not fair. I am saying what I understood him to say, and we will have to be judged by Hansard when it is issued. He certainly stated that he himself desired to appoint this gentleman that there might as a result be a cessation of certain articles of some kind, which articles he gave us to understand were objectionable to every one who wished the best interests of this country. I wish to place myself on record as disapproving of voting to a minister the people's money, to be used for such a purpose as that. If other people in this country are to be told that all they have to do in this country in order to get a fat Government job is to make a nuisance or a national peril of themselves, we will be a laughing stock in expending the people's money, and that is what we are as a Parliament and as a committee when we adopt the system by giving the minister the vote he asks. I am absolutely against giving the minister the money to be spent, when he declares that to be his policy. He has endeavoured to justify it by abuse of other people in the province of Quebec; far, far more than one-half the people in the province of Quebec have to-day had thrown at them from this Government the insult of being called disloyal in everything but in name. Absolutely, more than one-half of the people of Quebec. He says that the people of the province of Quebec who belong to the Liberal party were more disloyal than he himself was in 1911, and I say that is an insult to the great majority of his compatriots in the province of Quebec. I give that as my second reason for opposing this vote. I say that instead of being a reason to induce me to accept this vote it is a stronger reason for my not doing so. I wish to place myself on record as against voting any money to this hon. gentleman, not in a personal way to him, but I say that any minister of the Crown, speaking for himself and, for the time being, speaking for the Government, who says of his fellow British subjects in the province of Quebec that they are disloyal and that they desire to be opposed to Great Britain, our Mother Country, in this war -that he is a member of the Government whose influence makes towards disunity and discord and faction in the Dominion of Canada to-day, when above all else we need 
unity. And therefore I say that I not only oppose	giving	this vote to
the minister but I am opposed to joining, or co-operating, or concurring in any vote to this minister, so long as he throws this insult out, because so long as he is minister administering a department he is a standing offender against the people of that province. It was a very unfortunate remark. I think that it was the most terrible remark I have heard a minister make about other citizens of Canada since I have been in the House, saying what he has,said about the people of Canada in a day when we require harmony among ourselves, when we need all the unity we can have, because in unity there is strength. So, whether there is to be a division on this item or not, I place myself on Hansard as disassociating myself from this vote, disapproving of this vote, and of any vote wherein the hon. gentleman will have any part in the expenditure of the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I know my province better than the member who has just spoken.
Surely you do.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I know my people, too, and I tell him that the great majority of my people are as loyal to the British Empire and as anxious to help the Allies in this war as he himself or anybody in his riding.
You did not say that a minute ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is what I say, and I repeat it. I say that the Liberal press in Quebec, and I say the Liberal organization of the province of Quebec are playing politics only, politics first-and the press will prove it. I take up this paper, Le S'oleil, the strongest Liberal paper, the organ of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec. It is the organ of the Liberal party in the province of Quebec, as the Globe is the Liberal organ of the Liberal party in Ontario, or the Winnipeg Free Press the organ of the Liberal party in Manitoba.

The Globe does not always speak for the Liberal party, nor does the Winnipeg Free Press, nor does Le Soleil.
I represent a riding in that district, and Le Soleil never spoke for me, and I challenge the hon. gentleman to find a word from me in my career that will support the contention he has laid before you.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Does the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) say that Le Soleil is not the organ of the Liberal party?
I am not responsible for what Le Soleil says. It does not represent my views in any respect.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Does-
What the minister said was that the Liberal party in..Quebec was more disloyal than he had been. I do not know what Le Soleil says.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I hold in my hand the file of Le Soleil. At the top of the editorial page I find the words " Organ of the Liberal Party." And it is true. It is the organ of the Liberal party. What do you see in the Winnipeg Free Press, in the Toronto Globe? Those papers are recommending as strongly as possible to their party a support of conscription. Here is Le Soleil, of Quebec, which says last night:-
The French Canadian Conservatives only can save the country; their vote can kill conscription.
Here is an appeal in bold-faced letters made by Le Soleil of Quebec. And if you take Le Canada, another organ of the Liberal party in Quebec, you will see the same things repeated every day. And now take all of those meetings that we have in the province of Quebec-
Before the minister puts that away-

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I have the floor, and
it is my intention to defend myself.

I ask for a decision on
the ruling made by the House a short time ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I have been attacked,
and I am simply defending myself. The great majority of the population of my province is as loyal as the .majority of the people of any' other province in this country, but the trouble comes from certain people whom we have in Quebec at the present time. - The Liberal press, Le Canada of Montreal, Le Soleil of Quebec, Le Devoir and La Liberte of Montreal, have caused the trouble. Hon. gentlemen opposite will probably say they are my friends.

Sure-carried.
Mr. SEVJIGiNY:	You will see ;in Le
Devoir, Bourassa's paper, very strong attacks against the Minister of Inland Revenue, and you will see words of praise for Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I am told-I do not know whether I am right or not-that -these *words of praise in Le Devoir have only appeared since Sunday last. There was a
meeting recently in Montreal between Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Mr. Bourassa.
Who told you?
It is absolutely untrue.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: That is what I am told. The hon. member from Piotou says it is not correct.
Sir Wilfrid Laurier was not in Montreal last Sunday, he was in Ottawa.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I said they had an interview in Ottawa.
The hon. minister said Montreal.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I am told it was in
Ottawa.
Who told the hon. gentleman?

The statement which
the hon. gentleman from Moosejaw was so anxious to make, on which he dwelt so eloquently and forcibly, was that the hon. minister had committed the crime of saying that the Liberal party in Quebec was more disloyal than he was. In order to make any point of that statement, the hon. member from Moosejaw would have to accuse the hon. minister with being disloyal in 1911, because, if the hon. minister was not disloyal then there is nothing in the statement that the Liberal party was more disloyal than he. But he abandons all that argument, and goes into an harangue about the accusation against Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
Oration, if you please.

If the hon. gentleman
from Moosejaw and the members on the other side of the House want to invite comparison of the records of the party on this side of the House and the party opposite, they will get that record straight from the shoulder, and we will begin dealing with the records by referring to the leader of the Opposition, Sir Wilfrid Laurier. When members refer to the operations of men like Bourassa and Lavergne and others in Quebec, who have been preaching treason, let them look back on the record of their own leader, and they will find the counterpart for these treasonable utterances in the words uttered time and again by Sir Wilfrid Laurier. It does not lie in the mouth of the hon. gentleman from Kam-ouraska (Mr. Lapointe) to read a lecture to any person in this House. The hon. gentleman took an active part in Dorchester,

bringing forward a candidate who was preaching treason on the platform, hacked up by him and his leader. If these gentlemen desire to go into the records of their party, they will get all the record they want and more.

I should have been surprised if a debate took place in the House, in which the province of Quebec was in the limelight, without my hon. friend from Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) taking a part. He is always on hand when something is said about Quebec, especially if it is derogatory to that province.
What did I say against Quebec?

Neither the hon. gentleman nor anybody else would ever frighten me, or the people of my province, either in this House or -outside of it, and the sooner he takes that for granted the better. The hon. Minister of Inland Revenue quoted one Liberal newspaper (Le Soleil) as backing up what he said about the Liberal party in the province. He said, " Here is Le Soleil, the organ of the Liberal party, and here is what that paper says." Have hon. gentlemen found anything very extraordinary in the utterances of Le Soleil? He said the Manitoba Free Press was preaching for unity in the country, and Le Soleil and Le Canada were against conscription. Does my hon. friend take the position that any man in this country who is not in favour of conscription is not loyal? Does he say that the Liberals of Quebec are disloyal because they are opposed to conscription? I am opposed to conscription.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Order.

My hon. friend before indicting the Liberal party of Quebec, and charging Sir Wilfrid and the province with disloyalty, should have something else on which to base his statements than newspaper articles stating that the people were opposed to conscription.
Does the hon. minister say that, because a newspaper or individual opposes conscription therefore they are disloyal?
Is the hon. Secretary of State, who is opposed to conscription and has resigned his portfolio, disloyal?

We might get back to
business, and find out what the minister

is going to do about this appointment. Who is filling the office in the meantime?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Mr. Lemay.

Is he recommended by
the Civil Service Commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: He was in the department. He is an accountant, and the intention of the Civil Service Commission is to recommend him within six months.

How long hae Mr. Lemay
been assistant accountant?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: He came into the department two years- ago.

Does the minister think it
would he a good thing to adopt the principle of promotion in his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, .and that is what will ;be done in this case.

The question has not
yet 'been answered. Does the minister mean to say that opposition to conscription means disloyalty? That is a fair question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is. absolutely irrelevant.
I am hound to bow to youT ruling, but I wish to state my position.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Minister of Inland Revenue has been given a latitude to defend himself, because he felt he was accused, but all the discussion up to that point was absolutely out of order.
He gave the reasons why he made this appointment.

The Chairman has just
stated that the Minister of Inland Revenue, having been attacked, was given a great .deal of latitude-by the Chair in order to defend himself, which I think is quite proper, under the rules of the House. But in defending himself, should he be permitted to attack the whole .province and brand that province which he represents as disloyal?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I never did that.

He said the Liberal
press of Quebec were preaching disloyalty, because Le Soleil said the Liberal press was against conscription. He has been asked a fair question, whether a man opposed fo conscription is necessarily disloyal, and that has been ruled out of order. The general discussion which took place tins afternoon must have been in order,
I

or you, Mr. Chairman, would not have permitted it. The question which has been put to the minister, therefore, must be ia order. It is only fair to the province of Quebec that the minister should let us know whether or not he really thinks that that province is disloyal because it opposes conscription.
Will the minister answer the question?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: If the question were put in a fair way, I should be very glad to answer it.
Will the minister suggest a fair way?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have just said that the great majority of the people of my province are perfectly loyal.
The minister said that the Liberal party was disloyal.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I said the Liberal press.
Because it is opposed to conscription.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I did not say because it is opposed to conscription. I say that the Liberal press is trying to make trouble in the province of Quebec. I have not all the newspapers with me, hut here is one which was published last night-LeSoleil, of Quebec-which makes an appeal to the French Conservative members on this side of the House, saying they should kill conscription.
Is that disloyal?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I never said that Quebec was disloyal.
Is the statement in the press disloyal which the minister has just mentioned?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, it is.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I wish members of the committee to take note that this whole discussion is out of order and against the rules.
Will the minister explain why he did not recommend Mr. Lemay for promotion to the position of accountant?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: When I came into the department I was told that the position was vacant. I did not know at the time that Mr. Lemay was mentioned for promotion.
Who informed the minister that the position was vacant?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not remember.
Was the position vacant when the minister came into the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
What caused the vacancy?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The death of Mr. Vallin.
Did the minister ask his deputy, before he recommended Mr. Renault, what was the practice of the department with respect to promotions?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: When I came to the department in March or April last I said to Mr. Vincent, the deputy minister, that I had recommended Mr. Renault for the position of accountant in my department. If I remember rightly, Mr. Vincent mentioned to me the name of Mr. Lemay.
In what connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: For the position in question; but before I spoke to Mr. Vincent I had already recommended Mr. Renault.
Does the minister take any stock in promotions in his department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
Did he think of recommending any deserving official in his department instead of hunting up this poor, foresaken journalist in Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It was for-
Political Teasons?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The vacancy was mentioned to me before I had a conversation on the subject with the deputy minister. As I have said, Mr. Renault was recommended to me by good business men in Quebec city. I told them that if Mr. Renault was qualified to fill the position I would recommend his appointment.
Surely the minister does not take it for granted that he can run his department upon the recommendation of the good citizens of Quebec?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not.

I can quite understand
that the deputy minister would favour the appointment of an outsider, because he himself came into the department in the first instance to occupy the position which he now holds. I assume that the minister wishes to help the civil servants; if he does, he should consider the advisability of promoting deserving officials rather than taking men from outside for political reasons

simply because they are recommended by so-and-so.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is my intention to promote employees wherever possible.

I understand that the
minister has quite recently appointed to positions in his department three men from outside the service. I should be obliged if the minister would give us at eight o'clock a list of appointments made to the Inside Service in his department either by him or by his immediate predecessor, noting especially those brought in from the outside.
Who first suggested Mr. Renault to the minister as a competent person to fill the position of accountant?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not remember.
What salary attaches to the office?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue

speechtext: If I have enough money it is my intention to give an increase to all the employees of the Outside Service. But if I have not enough money I shall have to make a choice of the best employees.

This vote includes::-
Provisional allowance, not more than $150 each to officers In Manitoba and provinces west thereof, whose salaries do not exceed $2,500 per annum. (Weights and Measures!.
Why is not this made applicable to officers in the other provinces?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Such an allowance is not confined to my department, but applies to the Post Office and Customs Departments also. It is considered that the cost of living is higher in the West than in the East. But, in my judgment, the cost of living at present is as high in the East as in the West.

Whatever reason there may have been in former times for this discrimination, I am sure there is none at present. In the Maritime Provinces the cost of living has gone up twice as much as in any part of Canada. As the minister is making special provision for the officers in the Western provinces I think it only fair that similar provision should be made for thosfe in the East.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I am glad to hear the
hon. gentleman talk that way, and I hope that when my Supplementary Estimates are before the committee he will be willing to give me enough money to give increases to all the employees of my department throughout the Dominion.
Deserving and undeserving?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
They are all deserving;
otherwise we would not keep them.

In considering the merits of a member of the Inside Service, the minister has the advice of his deputy minister and of the head' of the branch. But hew does he get information as to the merits of officers in the Outside Service? I am afraid that in the Inland Revenue Department we shall see what we have seen in other departments-a certain class of the public servants are found to be most deserving, and others, for some reason, not so deserving. Up to 1911 the money was^ distributed equally, but since then, and* now, only a certain class can get it. I urge upon the minister that when he gives increases he should try to get some positive information about the officer concerned, so that there may be no unfair discrimination -that the rain, as it were may fall on the just and the unjust. I hope especially that *those who are receiving small salaries will be among those given increases, and that in dealing with this matter the minister will beware of the leaven of politics.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
When I receive a request for an increase of salary, I place it before my deputy minister, and if I decide to give an increase it is because it is re-

commended by the officers of the department. I can assure the hon. gentleman, Mr. McKenzie, that many of the employees who were in the department before 1911 have received some increases, when we have enough money to give them. This has been true under Mr. Blondin and Mr. Patenaude, and it is true under my own administration of the department.

I heard on very good authority that for the fifteen years that the Liberals were in power we had in some departments Tory heads who had a free hand, and who were giving preference to their Tory friends during those fifteen years. When the change came, matters became worse; we had not only a Tory deputy head bur a Tory head, so that it was a case of bringing in seven worse devils than there were before, and the class of civil servants to whom I have referred are getting it going and coming. If any deputy head or head of a department thinks he is doing these things under a bushel, I want the minister to know that we know about these things, and I hope that this manner of dealing with officials will not find place nor part in his department.

The minister has not told us the exact meaning of the two extra amounts he is asking for under this item. The minister is more extravagant in his department than any other minister. He is asking for an increase of $142,442.50 in excise, of $26,000 in weights and measures, and of $10,000 in adulteration of food. The weights and measures business of the country is surely not of such a pressing character in war time, when men have to be conscripted to win the war, that the minister should ask the people to be taxed this extra amount of $26,000. The same is true with regard to the adulteration of food item. Why should there be an increase of $36,000 in these two branches? The minister is asking for $10,000 for increases of salaries of officers, inspectors and assistant inspectors of weights and measures. He told us a few minutes ago that they were all statutory increases.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I made a mistake. I thought that was the Inside Service. There are no statutory increases for the Outside Service.
Will the minister give us the names of those whose salaries are to be increased?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Generally speaking, we desire to give an increase to every one of

our officials of the Outside Service, and I hope we shall have enough money for that.
Are you going to appoint any new officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: .That is not the intention of the department.
Have you appointed any new officers within the last six months?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Not in the weights and measures branch. Perhaps we have appointed a few men, but the appointments have been to fill vacancies.
I am speaking of additional appointments, not to fill vacancies.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
During the last six
months we have appointed, throughout the whole country, five or six men.
To new positions.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
Who are they?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I will get the names for my hon. friend.
Why should there be an increase of $15,000 in rent, fuel, travelling expenses, etc. for weights and measures?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We were given $65,000 last year by Parliament, but we were short by $15,000, and it is to cover that deficit that we are asking for $15,000 more this year.

I am at a loss to understand why in a department such as this of weights and measures where everything runs along in a groove absolutely certain and definite, that does not involve any eruptions of any kind in the service, the minister should require such an increased expenditure as $15,000 that could not be foreseen. I am at a loss to understand why his predecessor spent so much more money than was voted. We have received no explanation from the minister. The minister may be paying the penalty for the sins of his predecessor who has passed on to some other department. I can understand that in a department where flexible conditions exist, where unusual and unexpected demands may be made, a minister may be called upon to meet expenditures which, I presume, would have to pass the gauntlet of an Order in Council, and in such a case he might come with the explanation that the present minister has given. Either the minister's prede-
JUNE 15, Ifd7
cessor must have been a spendthrift, or the minister must have been. If the minister is going to spend $15,000 more, he should tell us what he is going to do with the money.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: When the amount of $65,000 was submitted to the minister, we thought that such an amount would be sufficient to meet all the requirements, but I understand that the department, as everybody else, has suffered on account of the high cost of everything. This item is for rent, fuel, travelling expenses, postage, stationery, etc., for weights and measures, including amount for purchase of standards of the metric system, salaries and other expenses of inspection. Last year we spent $80,000.

Where did you
get the money?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I am told that on the
6th of February of this year a vote was passed by this House, number 386, for rent, fuel, travelling expenses, postage, stationery, for weights and measures, including an amount for the purchase of standards of the metric system, salaries and other expenses, further amount required, $20,000. We required that amount to pay our officials, and we came before Parliament and were given the money.

As the hon. member for
Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) has already said, this is a department of service which has not been the subject of expansion for any special reason during the past several years. It is obvious that the predecessor of my hon. friend, for whose action he must answer to the House, simply went on and spent $15,000 that he had no authority to spend, that this House had not authorized him to spend.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We did not spend it until it was voted in the Supplementary Estimates.

The service was incurred before any Supplementary Estimates were voted. There has been no change of conditions that warranted such an expansion of expenditure; it was simply $15,000 of extravagant expenditure on the part of my hon. friend's predecessor in office. Last year Parliament was asked for a certain vote on the representation that that amount would be sufficient to carry this service through the year, and the department incurred this additional expenditure of $15,000. It is for the minister to show the committee, not only where he'spentthis
money, but why he spent this money. It is quite true that the over expenditure made by the department was provided for by Parliament, as the minister has said, by the passing of the extra Supplementary Estimate this year. But the committee are now asked to assent to the Main Estimates for the coming year, and this is the time and place when the Government ought to be prepared to state to the country, through the committee why an increase of expenditure has been made. Such explanations are not generally asked for or made on the occasion of what are called the extra Supplementary Estimates. Why was that expenditure made? Was it a provident, economical and necessary expenditure, or a wasteful, extravagant and unnecessary expenditure? The country is entitled to that information.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The greater expenditure was necessary on account of the increase in the service. The industry of the country, generally speaking, was never so prosperous as since the outbreak of the war, and owing to this great increase and development of industry in Canada, the weights and measures service has greatly increased. It is only on account of that increase that this additional amount has been required; there was no extravagant or useless expenditure.

The minister makes a
'broad, general statement that an increase in the cost of administration of the weights and measures naturally follows the expansion of industry. I am at one with the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) in the belief that it does not necessarily so follow. The provision for the inspection of weights and measures is made, and there would have to be a very large expansion of industry indeed to require a large further expenditure by the department in that connection.
That is, unless this minister acts on the principle that money is free just now, and that the Inland Revenue Department should spend money liberally, as other departments of the Government have done; and possibly the other departments have not been as severely criticised for it as they should have been. The lines of expenditure in the Inland Revenue Department are laid down very closely, and there is not the same occasion for expansion as in other departments. A general statement is not information. We should have a detailed statement as to what appointments it is necessary to make, whether they were made

and what they cost the country, because it appears to me that there has been a sufficient staff of weights and measures inspectors and officials of this department generally, as well as other departments of the government, appointed since 1911, to take care of any expansion of any industry which has taken place, or that we may hope to take place for a long time to come. In other words, the staff has been kept at full strength, and has been increased, although the business has admittedly gone down. That being the case, a general statement on the part of my hon. friend is not an explanation, and he should be prepared to give us the actual details as to how the increase took place.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I will not be able tonight to give my hon. friend all the details of that increase, but we have ' had that increase because it was required. I will have prepared in my department a detailed statement of all the increases that were required, and I hope that will be satisfactory to my hon. friend.

This large increase )of
$15,000 expenditure for this service apparently took place in the fiscal year ending 30th March, 1917. Will the minister be good enough to prepare the detailed statement as to the increase, and why it was necessary?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
The item will stand in order to get information.
Has the hon. minister the information he promised in regard to prosecutions for infraction of the War Stamp Act?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We prosecuted about 400 persons - for infraction of the Act all over the country. At first we were very lenient and our officers conducted a campaign of education, but since the war broke out we have instituted 400 prosecutions.
Does the department prosecute all persons against whom complaints are made?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes, through our officers.
Will the hon. gentleman have a list prepared of the complaints received in regard to parties who have violated the provisions of the Act, and a list of prosecutions?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.

I presume this is called preventive or detective work. Under what

system is the work performed and paid for? Is it by salaried officials permanently appointed by the department, or by men temporarily appointed, who work on commission, receiving a portion of the fine?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We have employees who receive an annual salary, and in each case the official is entitled to half the fine, in addition to their salaries.
In addition to salary and travelling expenses?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
Are these permanent or temporary employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Most of them are permanent.
About what is the average salary paid?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: $900 now. The officers say it is not enough, and desire an increase.

There was some complaint made in the House a little while ago by the member for West Kent (Mr. McCoig) in regard to the administration of this part of the Inland Revenue service. He complained of the character of the service rendered. I think that it is objectionable to pay for service of this character by giving a percentage of the fine. No doubt many unjustifiable cases occur under that system. Some of these cases were mentioned by the hon. gentleman from West Kent, which certainly reflected very seriously on the administration of the department. It is generally accepted that the principle of paying the informer a part of the fine is not a good one, and is not to the credit of those in authority who administer the law in that way. It would be very much better to employ more highly salaried officials, who would be men of higher standing and character, who would administer this part of the work of the department in a much more effective, and creditable manner.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The experience of the
department is that the present system is the most effective.
How many such appointees are there in the service of the department?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Over a hundred, all over the country.

I think the member for West Kent, in speaking of this matter, suggested that there were occasions, within his knowledge, in which the detective was the

instigator of the offence. What is the policy of the department in that connection? Does the department consider it legitimate for the detective to instigate the offence, or, in any degree, to become a party to it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: We have never credited that statement, and I certainly -would not tolerate such conduct. If the hon. gentleman has complaints to make against the officials who are doing that work, I would be very glad to receive them.

The member for West
Kent made certain complaints.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: It would be better if he would give the names. When did he make the complaints?

Last week, I think; it
is in Hansard.
, Mr. OLIVER:	He was discussing the
'possible regulation of cold storage and he instanced certain cases of hardship that had occurred under the administration of the Inland Revenue Department. It is not the policy of the department, then, to encourage this method of enforcing the regulations. How far would the department go in the way of discouraging such methods? Would they be willing to dispense with the services of a detective who had been a party to such a transaction?
Mr. SEVIGNY. Yes.
That is definite.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Yes.
Adulteration of food and the administration of tile Act respecting fertilizers, _ fraudulent marking and commercial feeding stufis, $50,000.

What is the work of the
department in this connection?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
Samples of food are collected 'by our officers throughout the country and sent to Ottawa, Halifax, Vancouver and Winnipeg for analysis. If they are adulterated, prosecutions aretaken against the persons offering such foods for sale.
. Mr. OLIVER:	There is an increase of
$10,000 in this vote. Is this a case of the expansion of industry?
. Mr. SEVIGNY:	Yes, the service is increasing very much. Last year we were voted $40,000, but we did not have enough money.

It is evident that the minister's Estimates are not properly prepared, and for this somebody in the department is censurable. For instance, why should $1.25,000 have been asked for last year for excise when $67,000 was enough to cover the expenditure for the year? This year the same amount is required. Some man in the department is responsible for this. Either the minister is not properly instructed, or he has not given enough attention to the preparation of his Estimates. Or, perhaps, the officers of his department do not properly prepare him for asking the committee to pass his Estimates.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: In the case of the item of $125,000, in 1916 the amount asked for was $175,000, and last year it was reduced to $125,000.

More ought to
come off.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
We shall probably have
to buy machines to emboss cheques; the matter is under consideration. We are required by the Banking Association to do that work, and it is practically decided that we shall have to buy the necessary machines.

I am disposed to be
generous with my hon. friend, because I know that he has not been long in office. But apparently his predecessor has overspent the money that was voted by Parliament. My hon. friend tells us that he wants $10,000 more under this 10 p.m. item, and so on^and this in respect of a department the operations of which are limited. What is the explanation of this $10,000 increase?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I shall be only too glad to give this information to the committee with the other information that I intend to bring down.

The main point is, why
was this over-expenditure made, and what, if any, justification was there for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I, will have a statement
prepared in my department.

In the three divisions of my hon. friend's department there are increases over and above the vote of Parliament and beyond what the minister says has been the increased expenditure. As the matter stands it simply means that my hon. friend's predecessor in office did not pay any regard to the vote of Parliament, but simply spent as much money as he desired and then asked Parliament to pay the bill. I submit that that is not a reasonable or proper way to administer the affairs of the country, and if the minister could

show that his predecessor did not conduct the affairs of the department in that way it would be very much to his credit. But according to the explanation of the minister the situation is as I have described, and it looks as if the minister having conducted the affairs of his department in that manner for a certain period, stepped put and allowed the mantle to fall on the shoulders of my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I think it would be more satisfactory for the committee to have a statement of the expenditure made on all these items. I have no hesitation in saying that my predecessor was very careful in the administration of his department, and it is my intention to be the same. Mistakes may have inadvertently been made in the preparation of the Estimates, and we are now asking Parliament for the necessary money. Instructions have been given to practise economy throughout the whole department, and it is certainly my intention to follow that practice particularly during the war.

The instructions cannot have been properly given because the conditions which hon. gentlemen have brought to the attention of the committee have evidently prevailed in the department for some time. At the beginning of the session supplementary Estimates were brought down to make up the deficiencies in the three branches of my hon. friend's department, Weights and Measures, Excise, and Adulteration of Food. Already this session $05,000 have been passed in that way, showing that these shortages in the Estimates at all events, have continued for some time.
I am pointing that out to my hon. friend that he may bear it in mind when he is preparing the statement he is to make to the committee.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: A mistake was made in the preparation of the Estimates last year, and as we do not wish to repeat the mistake this year. We are asking for an increased amount.
My hon. friend has not shown the committee that what he is asking for will be sufficient.

Without any facts before me I must say that it looks as if the officers of the department had not prepared the Estimates properly, and as if the department was badly administered. Does the minister know whether these officers know what Estimates mean? Perhaps they have the idea that they can spend as much 
money as they like, and then ask Parliament for money to liquidate the over-payment.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: After the explanation given by the Minister of Finance a few minutes ago, 1 think my hon. friend will appreciate that it is not an easy matter for the officers to spend as much as they like. I have been in the department only five months.
We are not criticising the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I have some very well qualified officials, and am perfectly satisfied with their services.
You should have been a little better posted.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I admit that. I shall be ready to give the committee all the information they desire when the Estimates are up again.

In Volume I of the Auditor General's Report for last year, in certain correspondence running from pages 537 to 543 between the Auditor General and the Inland Revenue Department, the Auditor General charges that quite a number of servants are being maintained by the department contrary to law. Perhaps when the minister's Estimates are up again he will explain why these assistants are kept on without having passed the proper examination. '

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I will make a note of it.
I know the minister has the horse races to-morrow on his mind, and I would suggest that the committee rise.

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I was entirely innocent of horse racing until my hon. friend put the notion in my mind. I have no objection to the committee rising.
Progress reported.
On the motion of Sir George Foster, the House adjourned at 10.15 p.m.
Monday, June 18, 1917.
